你: you (informal, as opposed to courteous 您)
呢: particle indicating that a previously asked question is to be applied to the preceding word ("What about ...?", "And ...?"); particle for inquiring about loc…
不客气: you're welcome; don't mention it; impolite
对不起: I'm sorry; excuse me; I beg your pardon; to let (sb) down; to disappoint
他: he; him (used for either sex when the sex is unknown or unimportant); (used before sb's name for emphasis); (used as a meaningless mock object)
请: to ask; to invite; please (do sth)
是: to be (followed by substantives only); correct; right; true; (respectful acknowledgement of a command) very well
不: no; not so; (bound form) not; un-
叫: to shout; to call; to order
认识: to know; to recognize; to be familiar with
的: of; ~'s (possessive particle); (used after an attribute); (used to form a nominal expression)
有: to have; there is; (bound form) having; with; -ful; -ed; -al (as in 意 intentional)
个: (classifier used before a noun that has no specific classifier); (bound form) individual
多: many; much; too many; in excess; (after a numeral) ... odd
大: big; large; great; older (than another person); eldest (as in 姐)
家: used in 家伙 and 家俱
这: (pronoun) this; these; (bound form) this; the (followed by a noun); (bound form) this; these (followed by a classifier) (in this sense, commonly pr. [zhèi], …
那: (specifier) that; the; those (colloquial pr. [nèi]); (pronoun) that (referring to persons, things or situations); then (in that case)
都: all; both; entirely; (used for emphasis) even; already
没: (negative prefix for verbs) have not; not
爱: to love; to be fond of; to like; affection; to be inclined (to do sth); to tend to (happen)
现在: now; at present; at the moment
星期: week; day of the week; Sunday
去: to go; to go to (a place); (of a time etc) last
来: to come; (used as a substitute for a more specific verb); hither (directional complement for motion toward the speaker, as in 回来)
北京: Beijing, capital of the People's Republic of China
吃: to eat; to consume; to eat at (a cafeteria etc); to eradicate; to destroy
想: to want to; would like to
to think (about); to think of; to devise; to think (that); to believe (that)
喜欢: to like; to be fond of
了: to finish; to achieve; to understand clearly
怎么样: how?; how about?; how was it?
块: lump; chunk; piece; classifier for pieces of cloth, cake, soap etc; (coll.) classifier for money and currency units
些: classifier indicating a small amount or small number greater than 1: some, a few, several
看: to see; to look at; to read; to watch
在: to exist; to be alive; (of sb or sth) to be (located) at; (used before a verb to indicate an action in progress)
住: to live; to dwell; to stay
上: (bound form) up; upper; above; previous; first (of multiple parts); to climb; to get onto; to go up
后面: the back; the rear; the last bit; behind; near the end; at the back; later; afterwards
工作: to work; (of a machine) to operate; job
做: to make; to produce; to write; to compose; to do; to engage in; to hold (a party etc)
回: to circle; to go back; to turn around
会: can; to have the skill; to know how to; to be likely to; to be sure to; to meet; to get together
读: to read out; to read aloud; to read; to attend (school); to study (a subject in school)
说话: to speak; to say; to talk
听: to listen to; to hear; to heed; to obey; a can (loanword from English "tin")
同学: to study at the same school; fellow student; classmate
热: to warm up; to heat up; hot (of weather)
看见: to see; to catch sight of
开: to open (transitive or intransitive); (of ships, vehicles, troops etc) to start; to turn on; to put in operation; to operate; to run
睡觉: to sleep; to go to bed
to go to bed; to sleep
喂: hey; to feed (an animal, baby, invalid etc)

grammar.title: Adjectives with 很
grammar.explain: Chinese adjectives don't need a word for 'am / is / are'. You just put 很 ('very') in front of the adjective. In short answers 很 is often not translated: 我很好 simply means 'I'm fine'.

grammar.title: Yes/no questions with 吗
grammar.explain: To turn a statement into a yes/no question, add 吗 at the end. The word order does not change. 你好吗 is a real question about how someone is, used with people you already know.

grammar.title: Bouncing a question back with 呢
grammar.explain: 呢 after a person means 'and you? / what about him?'. It repeats the question you were just talking about, so you don't need to say the whole question again.

questions.q: What does A invite B to do?

grammar.title: Linking nouns with 是
grammar.pattern: A + 是 + B　/　A + 不 是 + B
grammar.explain: 是 links two nouns, like 'am / is / are' in English. To say 'not', put 不 in front of 是. Don't use 是 with adjectives: say 我很好, not 我是好.

grammar.title: Question words stay in place
grammar.pattern: 你 叫 什么 名字 ？　/　他 是 谁 ？
grammar.explain: Chinese does not move question words to the front of the sentence. Put 什么 (what), 谁 (who) or 哪 (which) exactly where the answer will go. Questions with these words don't need 吗.

grammar.title: Possession with 的
grammar.explain: 的 works like English 's: 我的 = my, 老师的 = the teacher's. With close people, such as family and friends, 的 is often left out: 我朋友 'my friend'.

sentences.en: He's not a teacher, he's a student.

lines.en: Hi! I'm Wang Ming. What's your name?
I'm Chinese. Nice to meet you!

grammar.title: Counting from 1 to 99
grammar.explain: Chinese numbers are very regular. 11 is 十一 (ten-one), 20 is 二十 (two-ten), and 35 is 三十五 (three-ten-five). Once you know 0–10, you can say every number up to 99.

grammar.title: Number + measure word + noun
grammar.explain: Between a number and a noun, Chinese needs a measure word. 个 is the most common one and works with people and many things. (For 'two' before a measure word Chinese uses 两, which comes in Level 2.)

grammar.title: Asking about age
grammar.pattern: Subject + 几 岁 ？　/　Subject + 多 大 ？
grammar.explain: 几 asks about small numbers, so 几岁 is used with children. With adults, ask 多大 (how old). In the answer you just say the number + 岁, with no 是.

examples.en: How old are you? — I'm six.
How old are you? — I'm twenty.

sentences.en: How old are you? (to a child)
How many Chinese friends do you have?
Does he have a Chinese name?

lines.en: I'm nineteen. Do you have Chinese friends?
Yes, I have three Chinese friends.

questions.q: How many Chinese friends does B have?

grammar.title: This and that: 这 and 那
grammar.pattern: 这 / 那 + 是 + Noun　/　这 / 那 + 个 + Noun
grammar.explain: 这 means 'this' and 那 means 'that'. They can stand alone before 是, or come before a measure word and a noun: 这个人 'this person'.

grammar.title: Negating 有 with 没
grammar.explain: 有 ('to have / there is') is always made negative with 没, never with 不. 没有 means 'don't have' or 'there isn't'. A short answer to a 有 question is 有 or 没有.

examples.en: Do you have a daughter? — No, I don't.

grammar.title: 和 and 都
grammar.pattern: A 和 B + 都 + Verb / Adjective
grammar.explain: 和 joins nouns ('Dad and Mom'); it is not used to join two sentences. 都 means 'both / all' and always goes after the subject, right before the verb.

examples.en: My dad and mom are both doctors.

sentences.en: There are four people in my family.
How many people are in your family?
My family is Dad, Mom and me.
My dad and mom are both teachers.
I don't have a dog, I have a cat.
My daughter is little; she's five.

lines.en: This is my dad. He's a doctor.
How many people are in your family?

questions.q: How many people are in B's family?
What pet does B's family have?

grammar.title: Telling the time with 点
grammar.explain: 点 means 'o'clock'. Ask the time with 现在几点？ Words like 上午, 中午 and 下午 go before the time, not after it. (Two o'clock is 两点 — you'll meet 两 in Level 2.)

grammar.title: Dates go from big to small
grammar.pattern: Year 年 + Month 月 + Day 日 + 星期 …
grammar.explain: Chinese dates start with the biggest unit: year, then month, then day. Months are a number + 月, days a number + 日 (in speech people often say 号 instead). Days of the week are 星期 + a number: 星期一 is Monday … 星期六 is Saturday, and Sunday is 星期日.

grammar.title: Time words go before the verb
grammar.pattern: Subject + Time + Verb　/　Time + Subject + Verb
grammar.explain: When something happens comes before the verb — either right after the subject or at the very start of the sentence. It never goes at the end as it often does in English.

sentences.en: When are you going to Beijing?
Are you coming to my place at noon?
The teacher is coming at 4 p.m.
My mom is coming to Beijing on Saturday.

lines.en: When are you going to Beijing?

questions.q: When is B going to Beijing?

grammar.title: 想 + verb: would like to
grammar.explain: 想 before a verb means 'want to' or 'would like to'. It is a polite, everyday way to say what you want. The negative is 不想.

examples.en: What would you like to eat?

grammar.title: 喜欢: to like
grammar.explain: 喜欢 can be followed by a thing (喜欢茶) or by an activity (喜欢喝茶). Add 很 for "really like" and 不 for "don't like".

grammar.title: 太…了 and 怎么样
grammar.pattern: 太 + Adjective + 了　/　Suggestion + ， 怎么样 ？
grammar.explain: 太…了 means 'too …' or, when you are pleased, 'so …!': 太好了 'Great!'. 怎么样 asks 'how is it?', and after a suggestion it means 'how about it?'.

examples.en: How about we eat at a restaurant?

sentences.en: What would you like to eat?
What would you like to drink?
How about we eat at a restaurant?
What do you want for lunch?

lines.en: It's noon. What do you want to eat?
How about we eat at a restaurant?
What would you like to drink? Tea?
I don't drink tea. I'll have water.

questions.q: What does B want to eat?

grammar.title: Asking the price
grammar.pattern: Thing + 多少 钱 ？ — Number + 块
grammar.explain: 多少 asks 'how many / how much' and can be used for any number, big or small (几 is only for small numbers). 多少钱 means 'how much money'. In everyday speech prices are given in 块.

grammar.title: Measure words 本 and 些
grammar.pattern: 这 / 那 / 一 + 本 + 书　/　这些 · 那些 · 一些 + Noun
grammar.explain: Many nouns have their own measure word: books use 本. 些 means 'some' and makes 这 and 那 plural: 这些 'these', 那些 'those', 一些 'some'.

examples.en: I want to buy a book.
I'd like to buy some fruit.

grammar.title: Doubling a verb: 看看
grammar.explain: Saying a verb twice makes it softer and shorter: 看看 means 'take a look'. It sounds relaxed and polite, which is perfect in a shop.

examples.en: Take a look at this book.

sentences.en: What do you want to buy?
I want to buy a few things.
I'd like to buy a book.
How many books do you want to buy?
How much money do you have?
This shop has lots of things.
There aren't many people in that shop.
I'd like to buy some apples.
I don't want to buy anything.

lines.en: Hello, how much is this book?

questions.q: How much is the first book?

grammar.title: 在: where something is
grammar.explain: 在 means 'to be at / in'. Ask where with 在哪里？ (哪里 = where). To say someone is not there, use 不在.

examples.en: The hospital is behind the school.

grammar.title: Location words come after the noun
grammar.pattern: Noun + 上 / 里 / 前面 / 后面
grammar.explain: To say 'on the table' or 'in the cup', put the location word after the noun: 桌子上 (table-on), 杯子里 (cup-in). To say what is somewhere, start with the place and use 有: 桌子上有一本书.

examples.en: The book is on the table.
There's a book on the table.

grammar.title: Where you do something
grammar.pattern: Subject + 在 + Place + Verb　/　住 在 + Place
grammar.explain: When 在 + place comes before another verb, it tells you where the action happens: 我在医院工作 'I work at a hospital'. With 住 ('live'), the place usually comes after it: 我住在北京.

sentences.en: The hospital is behind the school.
The train station is just ahead.
The shop is in front of the train station.
The book is on the table.
There's a book on the table.
There's a cup on the chair.
What do you do for a living?
My mom works at a school.
He's not home; he's at the hospital.
He's going back to China next week.
I was in Beijing last month.

lines.en: Excuse me, where is the train station?
The train station is behind the hospital.

questions.q: What does A ask about first?

grammar.title: 会: can (a learned skill)
grammar.explain: 会 means 'know how to' — for skills you have learned, like speaking a language or writing characters. The negative is 不会. Later you will also see 会 used for 'will (probably)'.

grammar.title: 能: can (be able to / be allowed)
grammar.explain: 能 means you are able to do something because circumstances allow it, or that it is allowed. Use it for 'Can you come tomorrow?' or 'Can I sit here?'. The negative is 不能.

grammar.title: 怎么 + verb: how to do something
grammar.explain: Put 怎么 ('how') right before a verb to ask how something is done. These two questions are very useful when you meet a new character.

examples.en: How do you read this character?
How do you write this character?

sentences.en: I can speak a little Chinese.
How do you read this character?
How do you write this character?
I can write my Chinese name.
I like listening to him talk.
Can you come to school tomorrow?
My computer is on the desk.

lines.en: A little. I study Chinese at school.
I can write some. How do you read this character?

grammar.title: 了: something has happened
grammar.explain: 了 at the end of a sentence shows that something has happened or that a situation has changed: 下雨了 'it's (started) raining'. To say something did not happen, use 没 before the verb and drop 了.

grammar.title: Getting around with 坐
grammar.explain: 坐 ('to sit') is also the verb for taking a taxi, plane or bus. The vehicle comes first and the destination after 去.

examples.en: I'm taking a taxi to the train station.

grammar.title: How long: Verb + time
grammar.explain: To say how long you did something, put the length of time after the verb (and after 了), but before the object.

examples.en: I watched TV for twenty minutes.

sentences.en: It's so cold in Beijing today!
I'm going to make a phone call.
We're taking a taxi to the train station.
What time do you go to bed?
I want to go to bed now.
I watched TV for twenty minutes.
It rained yesterday, so I didn't go to school.

lines.en: Hi, Anna! What's the weather like in Beijing?
It's raining in Beijing, and it's cold.

questions.q: What's the weather like in Beijing?
